question: What did Judas do with the silver?
summary: Matthew 27:5 has Judas throw the thirty pieces of silver down in the temple and then hang himself; the priests use the money to buy the Potter's Field. Acts 1:18 says Judas himself bought a field with the reward of iniquity and then fell headlong, bursting open with his bowels gushing out. Same character, same money, two incompatible accounts of who bought what field and how Judas died.

reconcile.connective: A study note catalogs the three concrete differences between Matthew and Acts before arguing Acts narrates only the aftermath of what Matthew describes.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman (The Lost Gospel of Judas Iscariot) argues the two death accounts are irreconcilable as they stand — both cannot be historically true.

pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact discrepancy under the heading "Judas' death — the manner. A diverse statement," harmonizing the hanging (Matt 27:5) with the fall and rupture (Acts 1:18) as one event: the rope or limb gave way and Judas fell onto rocks below, citing Prof. Hackett's on-site inspection of the terrain above the valley of Hinnom (pp. 349-350).

excerpts.excerpt_text: There are two accounts of Judas’s death—this one and Acts 1:18-19. There are differences between the two: (1) Matthew states that the priests bought the field (Matt 27:6-7), while Acts seems to suggest that Judas bought it (Acts 1:18); (2) Matthew reports that Judas committed suicide by hanging himself (Matt 27:5), while Acts enigmatically refers to a fall and an abdominal rupture (Acts 1:18); (3) Matthew implies that the field of blood was so named because it became a place of burial (Matt 27:7-8), while Acts suggests that it was because of Judas’s violent death there (Acts 1:19). The two accounts are compatible if one takes the account in Acts as describing the effects of the actions described in Matthew.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Note explicitly lists the three specific factual differences between Matthew and Acts on Judas's death (who bought the field, manner of death, why the field was named 'blood') and then argues they can be read as compatible — directly on the row's stated tension.
